story: Two months into the shot, she pulls a clump of hair from the shower drain.
Eating a fraction of what she used to, she's asleep on the couch by 7:30.
She's losing weight on the shot and worried she's losing nutrients with it.
Her post-op labs come back low again, even though she does everything right.
Since the surgery she's exhausted, and standard iron and B12 pills aren't absorbing.
Her part keeps widening and her ponytail is half the thickness it was.
Her doctor says her ferritin is normal, yet she's exhausted and still shedding.
She wants to feel like herself again, with energy and thick hair.
She has taken biotin gummies for six months and her shedding hasn't slowed.
Every hair vitamin ad promises thick hair, and she's stopped believing them.
Her doctor calls her ferritin of 20 normal, but she knows something is off.
She Googles hair loss causes at midnight, afraid it's permanent and nobody's looking.
She stares at the iron bottle she quit after weeks of stomach pain.
She remembers the constipation and nausea and won't try another iron pill.
She wants iron that doesn't wreck her stomach so she can get her energy back.
The donor center checks her hemoglobin, never her ferritin, while her stores empty.
She's proud to donate and wants to keep going without running on empty.
Reading his medication's side-effect sheet, he wonders if B12 explains his tingling.
Doctors call his brain fog normal for his age, and he doesn't buy it.
She snaps at her partner over nothing and wonders who she's turning into.
She wakes at 3am drenched, then drags through the next day.
She wants to feel like herself again before menopause hits full force.
Day two of her period, she cancels plans and white-knuckles through work.
Every cycle takes more iron than her diet replaces, and she's wiped out.
Years of heavy periods and now her hair is thinning, too.
She drinks collagen daily for hair and skin, and sees nothing change.
She learns her collagen scoop is an incomplete protein and feels played.
Her third gritty powder is sitting in the pantry, half-finished and hated.
She wants real nutrition in one easy capsule instead of another scoop.
A new breakout appears the morning of her big meeting, again.
She reads Accutane side-effect threads at midnight, desperate for another option.
Retinol leaves her skin red and peeling, and she's tired of the purge.
She wants vitamin A from food instead of another cream on her face.
Third coffee in hand, she's still dragging at 3pm.
She blanks on a colleague's name in the middle of a meeting.
She learns most of her $99 greens powder's ingredients don't list doses.
She's tired of spending $99 a month on a gritty drink.
She finds out her greens powder left out iron, B12 and vitamin A.
At 4am in the break room, she opens her third energy drink.
Night shifts and vending-machine meals leave her running on empty nutritionally.
Monday morning he sees a puffy, red face after a weekend of drinks.
He wonders what a weekend of drinking is doing to his liver.
Monday is a write-off, with the hangover fog lasting well into the afternoon.
His beer belly keeps growing, and he's quit on every diet.
His doctor flags his liver enzymes, and he isn't ready to quit beer.
She pours the nightly glass while packing lunches, then wakes up dull and puffy.
One or two glasses nightly, and she wonders what it's draining from her.
She wakes unrefreshed every morning no matter how early she goes to bed.
The belly won't budge, though he eats better and trains.
His doctor mentions a fatty liver, and he wants to fix it with food.
Keto, calorie counting and cleanses have all failed, and the weight keeps coming back.
Diet pills and shakes haven't worked, so a real food fix sounds right.
He eats steak and eggs but wonders if he's missing what organ meats give.
He avoids anything synthetic and wants supplements made from real food.
Every supplement label gets read, and anything with fillers goes back on the shelf.
Price per serving gets compared across brands before anything goes in the cart.
Liver is called a superfood, but cooking and eating it is a nonstarter.
A friend swears by liver capsules, so curiosity wins out over skepticism.
She starts a 'preparing for baby' shelf and wants food-form nutrients.
Another negative test on cycle eight, and she wonders if synthetic prenatals are enough.
Pumping at 2am on crackers alone, she's running on empty.
Months after birth, handfuls of hair are coming out in the shower.
Nursing and sleepless, she's depleted and has no time to cook.
